evidence: Sall. Jug. 31.13: caedem in aliquem facere
terms.comment: The usual classical word for a killing, of one person or many: murder, massacre, slaughter in battle. To commit murder is caedem facere (Sall. Jug. 31.13) or committere (Quint.); to murder someone, occīdere or interficere (see kill).
Death by violence, seen from the victim’s side; outside fixed phrases (vītae necisque potestās, power of life and death, Caesar) mostly in poetry. Traupman gives it for murder.

evidence: Quint. 3.10.1: sī quis homicīdiī accūsētur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The term of the courts from Quintilian on; Cicero says caedēs and, of the charge, inter sīcāriōs.
Cicero sets it beside sīcārius, an assassin who uses a dagger, and parricīda, the murderer of a parent or kinsman (Phil. 2.30–31).
From sīca, a dagger, but used of any murderer (Quint. 10.1.12). Inter sīcāriōs accūsāre, dēfendere: on a charge of murder (Cic. Rosc. Am. 90).

phrases.latin: In hōc librō dē caede quaeritur.
phrases.english: This book is a murder mystery.
